title: Themistocles Turns Silver Into Ships
text:
In the 480s BC the Athenians struck a rich new vein of silver in the state mines at Laurion, in southern Attica. The revenue was large, and the popular plan was to share it out among the citizens, about ten drachmas each.

Herodotus says that Themistocles persuaded the assembly to do something else. Instead of dividing the money, Athens should use it to build two hundred warships. His argument was not about Persia, which seemed distant, but about Aegina, the nearby island with which Athens was then at war and whose navy dominated the local waters. That was an enemy every citizen could see.

The assembly agreed, and the ships were built. A few years later, in 480 BC, Xerxes invaded Greece with a vast army and fleet. Athens had the largest navy among the Greeks, and those triremes formed the core of the fleet that fought at Artemisium and won at Salamis. Herodotus judged that the war with Aegina saved Greece by forcing Athens to become a sea power, and the navy built from the Laurion silver became the base of Athenian power for the rest of the century.
lesson: A windfall is a chance to build lasting strength rather than to spend for comfort today. Frame a long-term investment in terms people can feel now.
source: Herodotus, Histories 7.144; Plutarch, Life of Themistocles 4
caveat: Plutarch gives one hundred ships instead of the two hundred in Herodotus.
